articles.title: Everything you need to make homemade cookies that look and taste like they came from a bakery
articles.summary: Professional bakers break down everything you need to make homemade cookies, especially during the holidays. Here are their top tips for beginner to advanced bakers.
articles.body: Cookies are one of the most low-stress, beginner-friendly desserts you can make, and they’re always a crowd pleaser whether they melt in your mouth or crunch as you take a bite. There’s room to grow, too — as you become confident in the kitchen, you can pick more complex recipes that require a bit more skill. If you, like me, are gearing up for a holiday season that involves lots of cookie baking, read on. I talked to professional bakers about each step of the process and the best cooking baking tools to use. As an avid baker myself, I also added some of the tips and tricks I swear by. Plus, experts answered some of the most frequently asked questions about baking cookies, including what’s likely your biggest concern: how to avoid a burnt batch. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. How to make cookies, step by step Step 1: Make the cookie dough Once you decide what type of cookie you’re making (learn about some of the most common ones here), it’s time to put the dough together. First thing’s first: read through the entire recipe and follow it exactly as it’s written, as obvious as that sounds, says Penny Stankiewicz, a chef-instructor of pastry and baking arts at the Institute of Culinary Education. Don’t substitute ingredients — if you do, your cookies won’t taste or have the same texture as the recipe intended. There’s one exception to the rule: You can play with a recipe’s flavors and mix-ins. “As long as you don’t mess with the structural ingredients of the recipe, like flour, butter and sugar, you’re not going to wreck its integrity,” says Stankiewicz. “For example, you can change how much vanilla extract you add, sprinkle cinnamon into your dough or use two types of chocolate chips instead of one.” Below are tools experts recommend using while making cookie dough. Kitchen scale or measuring cups You can measure ingredients by volume or by weight. Measuring by volume involves using liquid and dry measuring cups, while measuring by weight involves using a kitchen scale. Arlyn Osborne, a recipe developer, food writer and the author of “Sugarcane,” recommends measuring ingredients by weight since it’s more precise and helps ensure that cookies are consistent every time you make them. Hand mixer or stand mixer The majority of cookies home bakers make involve the creaming method, which means the first step in the recipe is to cream room temperature butter and sugar together, says Stankiewicz. Using a stand mixer with the paddle attachment is the easiest way to do so. Experts also recommend keeping a flexible silicone spatula on hand to periodically scrape the sides of the bowl. You can use a hand mixer or spoon to cream butter and sugar for cookies, but it’s not as efficient. Mixing bowls Mixing bowls are available in materials like glass, ceramic and metal, but it ultimately doesn’t matter when it comes to making cookies, says Elizabeth Barbone, a recipe developer and cookbook author who runs the sites Cook Fast, Eat Well and Gluten-Free Baking. What does matter is the mixing bowl’s size. Ingredients spill out of bowls that are too small while you’re stirring, and while there’s no such thing as a bowl that’s too big while you’re hand-mixing, there is if you’re using a stand mixer. Mixing bowls that are too big may prevent the mixer’s paddle from reaching its sides, smearing ingredients into a paste along the bottom of the bowl instead of whipping it until fluffy, says Barbone. Step 2: Shape the cookies Each type of cookie has a signature shape (learn more about here), which you achieve using specific tools. Below, I listed what you need to form a few popular ones. Cookie scoop Cookie scoops help you create balls of dough for drop cookies that are the exact same size, ensuring that the batch bakes evenly, says Barbone. She prefers cookie scoops with trigger handles since they quickly release balls of dough, which makes shaping drop cookies fast and efficient. Cookie scoops come in a variety of sizes, which you’ll see listed as a number that corresponds to the number of scoops per quart of dough. For example, a #40 scoop gives you about 40 scoops per quart and a #10 scoop gives you about 10 scoops per quart — this means the #10 scoop is larger than the #40 scoop. There’s no standard scoop size you should look for, but #40 is common for cookies, says Barbone. If you make cookies often, consider buying a large, medium and small scoop so all your bases are covered. Rolling pin You don’t technically need to buy a rolling pin since you can use household objects as alternatives, like wine bottles and canned foods. But a rolling pin gives you more even results while making cutout cookies, so if you plan on baking often, it’s nice to have. Cookie cutters Cookie cutters come in hundreds of shapes: circles, hearts, squares, gingerbread men, menorahs, animals, numbers, letters, symbols… you name it, there’s a cookie cutter for it. Some companies even let you create custom cookie cutters, which is a great option for themed events. There’s options made from plastic and metal, either of which will do, but each material has strengths and weaknesses. Metal cookie cutters give cookies clean, crisp edges and they’re easy to clean since you can put them in the dishwasher, says Barbone. But they’re sharper compared to plastic cutters, so they’re not kid-friendly. Metal cookie cutters are also quite durable, says Stankiewicz. If you care for them properly, they can last for decades. In fact, Stankiewicz says her family’s copper cookie cutters have been passed down for generations.Plastic cookie cutters are duller compared to metal options. This makes them suitable for kids, but they can give cookies messy, smushed edges, says Barbone. Even if the plastic cookie cutters you buy say they’re dishwasher safe, it’s best to hand-wash them, says Stankiewicz — heat from the dishwasher can cause them to melt or become misshapen. Cookie press A cookie press, which you use to make spritz cookies, is a cylindrical tool with a plunger on one end and interchangeable discs on the other. Each disc has cutouts on it, creating different shapes. You load dough into the body of the press and use the plunger to push it through the disc’s holes, resulting in perfectly shaped cookies. You move the press’ head along the sheet pan and push out one cookie at a time. Barbone recommends buying a cookie press that comes with metal discs, which cleanly release dough so each cookie’s shape is clearly defined. Avoid plastic cookie presses: They’re more prone to getting clogged and breaking, she says. Plastic cling wrap (or a reusable alternative) After rolling dough into logs while making slice-and-bake cookies, you wrap each one in plastic cling wrap and put them in the refrigerator for a few hours or overnight. The plastic wrap keeps the dough fresh while it’s chilling and keeps odors and moisture out. If you’re looking for a plastic wrap alternative, reusable beeswax wrap is a great option, and some brands make silicone tools to help you size, shape and store slice-and-bake dough. Step 3: Bake the cookies Putting cookies in the oven is often the most nerve-wracking step for home bakers — no one wants to put effort into perfecting dough and end up with a burnt final product. To ensure cookies come out golden brown and ready to sink your teeth into, use the below expert-recommended tools. Oven thermometer Even when you set your oven to a specific temperature, it probably doesn’t warm up to exactly where you want it, unless it was recently calibrated, says Stankiewicz. This means your baked goods are likely cooking at a slightly lower or higher temperature than you’re anticipating, which impacts cooking time. To confirm that your oven reaches the right temperature before adding your cookies, Stankiewicz recommends buying an oven thermometer. It hooks onto the oven’s racks and reads its internal temperature, which you can monitor while your oven is preheating to adjust its settings accordingly. Sheet pans Experts recommend keeping a few half-sheet pans in your kitchen at all times because they’re so versatile. You can use them to bake and cook sweet and savory foods, plus they last for years if cared for properly. For cookies specifically, it’s best to use rimmed sheet pans. “I never use a sheet pan without a rim because there’s always a chance something could slide off the edge,” says Barbone. This is especially the case with cookies. Recipes often tell you to rotate the sheet pan halfway through to ensure all of the cookies bake evenly, and if your sheet pan doesn’t have a rim, the cookies may slide off during this process. Additionally, pay attention to the color of your sheet pan. Darker sheet pans tend to conduct more heat, which means the bottoms of your cookies will bake faster than the tops, says Stankiewicz. This is often why people end up with cookies that are burnt on the bottom but still raw on top. Use a lighter colored sheet pan to avoid this issue, says Stankiewicz. Parchment paper Parchment paper and silicone baking mats serve the same purpose and are essentially interchangeable when it comes to baking cookies. They line your sheet pan, provide a nonstick surface to bake on and make cleanup a breeze. You can also line your pan with tin foil, but since the material conducts heat, it tends to make the bottoms of your cookies darker and speed up baking time — try to avoid it if you can, says Sarah House, the food innovation chef and recipe and development lead at Bob’s Red Mill. Beyond one being disposable and the other being reusable, the main difference between parchment paper and silicone baking mats is how much cookies grip onto them. Silicone baking mats are so nonstick that cookies don’t have much to grasp onto, which might cause them to spread too much while baking, says Barbone. Parchment paper is still nonstick, but cookies can grip to it more, reducing spread. Barbone opts for parchment paper instead of silicone baking mats for cookies, but it’s ultimately a personal preference. Timer Always keep track of how long cookies have been in the oven relative to the estimated bake time detailed by your recipe. You can use a mechanical or digital timer, or devices like your phone or watch. Remember that a recipe’s estimated bake time is just a guideline, says Stankiewicz. Factors like the type of oven you’re using, whether you preheated it and how many trays of cookies are baking at once can impact baking time. Because of this, one of the best ways to determine cookie doneness is by using your nose. “Once you start smelling the cookies, start checking on them,” says Stankiewicz. From there, pay attention to the cookies’ color and texture. Fully baked cookies are usually golden brown and have a matte rather than glossy appearance, so once you see those signs and smell them, pull them out of the oven. Step 4: Let the cookies cool When you take your cookies out of the oven, let them cool on the sheet pan for five to 10 minutes before gently moving them to a cooling rack with a spatula, says House. If you leave cookies on a hot pan, they’ll continue baking and can become overdone. But placing cookies on a cooling rack allows air to circulate around them, cooling them quickly and preventing extra baking. Step 5: Decorate the cookies Once the cookies are cool, decorate them however you’d like, although it’s not a required step — they’re delicious straight out of the oven. A few ideas: you can dust your cookies with powdered sugar, make a glaze or frosting or top them with sprinkles. Step 6: Store the cookies As long as you bake cookies all the way through, the experts I talked to say most batches have a week-long shelf life. Store them in a container with a tightly sealed lid to keep air, odors and moisture out, and stack them with parchment paper between each layer so they don’t stick together. If you need to store fully baked cookies beyond a week, Barbone recommends freezing them. The best way to do so is by laying the cookies out on a sheet pan or plate and putting them in the freezer. Once they’re frozen, transfer them to an airtight container or a tightly sealed bag. Frozen cookies keep well for at least three to five months, says Osborne. What are the most popular types of cookies? Drop cookies: As the name implies, you make drop cookies by dropping balls of dough onto a sheet pan. The dough spreads in the oven, giving the cookies a round shape once baked — think typical chocolate chip cookies, for example. Drop cookies are the easiest cookies to make.Cut out cookies: The star of any holiday cookie box, cut out cookies are made by rolling out dough and using cookie cutters to create shapes. They’re also a great option for beginner bakers. People traditionally make cut out cookies from sugar or gingerbread cookie dough, but the flavor possibilities are endless. Slice-and-bake cookies: To make slice-and-bake cookies, you roll dough into logs and refrigerate them. Once the dough is chilled, you slice the logs into rounds and bake them on a cookie sheet. Slice-and-bake cookies are shortbread cookies, meaning they’re buttery and have a crumbly texture. They’re pretty straightforward to make.Spritz cookies: You make spritz cookies with a cookie press, a tool that pushes dough through a patterned disc. The dough is very soft, which makes it easy to force through the press. Once they bake, spritz cookies have a lighter texture compared to cut out cookies, says Barbone. Using a cookie press can be tricky, so experts recommend mastering more beginner-friendly bakes first, like drop, cut out and slice-and-bake cookies. Experts’ top cookie baking tips Throughout their years of baking cookies, the experts I talked to have seen and experienced their fair share of mistakes. Below are their tips for avoiding common issues. Cookie dough easily sticks to your rolling pin and countertop. To prevent this, people often sprinkle flour on the dough and surface its resting on, but doing so adds flour to the dough and too much can dry it out. Instead, Stankiewicz recommends rolling out the dough between two pieces of parchment paper to prevent sticking.If you’re measuring dry ingredients by volume, spoon them into measuring cups until they dome over the top. Then scrape a knife along the top of the measuring cups to level them off, says Osborne. This helps you avoid adding excess ingredients to your dough.The bottoms of cookies can burn for a number of reasons, but if you notice it happening every time you use a specific sheet pan, odds are the pan is too thin. Thin sheet pans transfer too much heat to cookies’ bases, causing them to bake faster than the rest of the treat and get darker at the bottom. Instead of buying a new set of pans, consider stacking two on top of each other, says Osborne. Doing so adds an extra layer of protection for the cookies’ bases since the two pans absorb double the amount of heat.To keep cookies soft, add a piece of white bread to the container you’re storing them in. The bread releases moisture inside the container, which the cookies slowly absorb so they don’t dry out. Replace the piece of bread every two days.If drop cookies lose their round shape in the oven, it’s fixable. Cookies are soft and moldable when they’re hot, so you can adjust them slightly, turning them back into a perfect circle. Take a circular cookie cutter or cup that fits over your cookies and gently swirl it around each one immediately after removing the pan from the oven, says Stankiewicz. Meet our baking experts At NBC Selected, we work with experts who have specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience. We also ensure that all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and with no undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. Elizabeth Barbone is a recipe developer and cookbook author who runs the sites Cook Fast, Eat Well and Gluten-Free Baking.Penny Stankiewicz, a chef-instructor of pastry and baking arts at the Institute of Culinary Education.Sarah House is the food innovation chef and recipe and development lead at Bob’s Red Mill. Arlyn Osborne is a recipe developer, food writer and the author of “Sugarcane.” Why trust NBC Selected? I’m a reporter at NBC Selected who’s written about kitchen tools for over six years, including articles about pie baking tools, Dutch ovens, nonstick cookware and plastic-free cutting boards. I’ve also been an avid baker for over a decade. To write this article, I interviewed four professional bakers about their favorite cookie baking tools and tips. I curated a list of their recommendations, and I also added products that I swear by after testing them. Of the injured, 11 were seriously hurt, while 21 suffered minor injuries.Police and fire department personnel were working to rescue people and provide temporary shelter to those who had lost their homes. Rescue teams were also putting up tents to accommodate residents displaced by the earthquake.According to the United States Geological Survey (USGS), the earthquake occurred at 10.33 pm local time, with its epicentre about 191 kilometres east-north-east of Nagqu. The area is sparsely populated and lies at a high altitude in northern Tibet. The USGS estimated the quake's depth at 18 kilometres below the Earth's surface.Nagqu lies more than 300 kilometres north of Lhasa, the capital of Tibet. articles.title: Hamilton Recalls Meets for African GP as He Makes Call for ‘Congo, Sudan, Syria, Palestine’
articles.summary: Lewis Hamilton is pleased to see the African GP make a return to the F1 calendar, but he has reservations about Rwanda amid calls for ‘free Congo, free Sudan...
articles.body:
Lewis Hamilton is pleased to see the African GP make a return to the F1 calendar, but he has reservations about Rwanda amid calls for 'free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine'.

Between the races in Singapore and Austin, the FIA, together with FOM, announced the return of the African GP to the F1 calendar from the early 2030s , after signing a long-term deal with the Rwandan government under the Visit Rwanda banner.

Even though Rwanda is a regional African nation, it has taken up the 'African GP' name, which holds a larger commercial value . Naturally, Ferrari's Hamilton is pleased to see the return of the Grand Prix that he had been pushing for several years.

Hamilton Recalls Countless Meetings to Push Africa Back on F1 Calendar

He revealed numerous calls made to Stefano Domenicali and even various heads of African nations. "I've been advocating for a race in Africa for many, many, many years," Hamilton said in the press conference ahead of the F1 US GP. "I have had countless meetings with the stakeholders, so many meetings with Stefano at his office in London, but also race weekends.

"Countless calls. 'What's happening?', 'where are we going?', 'who are you meeting with?'. Many meetings with different presidents from different countries, lots of phone calls with different presidents in different countries within Africa. For me, it's a place that deserves to have a Grand Prix.

"It's [about] more than just one country; it is about the continent in itself, and there are so many beautiful countries within it, and the people are so lovely. The culture is so rich, and I think it's important that we get to show that to the world, and we get to do that with our sport.

"We get to go to all these different countries, and people see some of these countries they didn't really know too much about and all of a sudden it's on the screen, and kids are talking about it. They go to school talking about it. So, I'm really, really hopeful for that Grand Prix," summed up Hamilton.

Amnesty International On Rwanda Situation With Congo

But Rwanda potentially hosting an F1 Grand Prix has certainly ruffled a section, especially the Democratic Republic of Congo. Amnesty International believes that Rwanda is undertaking war crimes together with the M23 militia in Congo.

They are committing horrific human rights abuses, targeting miners in Congo for gold and cotton. The items are trafficked across the border into Rwanda, with M23 acting as the enforcer at the behest of the Rwandan government.

Hamilton is aware of the news and is hopeful that African nations can unite as one in the future. He knows he can't neglect what is happening not just in Africa but around the globe. In fact, he made the call in the FIA press conference, which often tries to keep it apolitical, even though the call for humanity shouldn't be mixed with politics.

Hamilton is Aware as He Makes a Rare Call Using FIA Platform

Hamilton also pushes for more knowledge about various historical happenings around the globe that are not taught in schools in England. "Of course, I don't get to choose where we go, and naturally there are problems all over the world today," he continued. "I've seen many of the stories, but I think we really have to approach it with humility.

"There's a lot that we don't know. Growing up in England, they never ever taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum: a lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism and the West intervening. But if you see people, you see so many designs that are out there today; top brands come from Africa, and it's got all the richest resources.

"I really hope, and I still have hopes, that Africa unites. I know there are many people that don't want that to happen because they would be so powerful if they did, but I'm still hopeful that at some stage they will. Of course, going doesn't mean that you neglect the things that are happening there.

"So, hopefully many people will start to educate themselves a little bit more about what is happening there, what has happened there for hundreds of years, and I hope that does spark the conversation. I guess I'll finish it off with: I think we need to make sure we're pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there's a lot of peace that I'm hoping that at some stage we get to," summed up Hamilton.

Hamilton Hopes to Be Racing Until 2030 to be Able to Race in Africa

While he is happy that Africa is finally making a return, he joked about having to stay fit until the 2030s and keep racing to be part of the returning F1 African GP. It is still about four seasons away, and Hamilton is already 41 years old. He will be 45 years old by the time the first race takes place.

"I mean, I'm now forced to have to stay a lot longer, because we have a race in Africa," said Hamilton. "And that's been my dream to be able to race in Africa. I mean, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit if I can. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we'll keep it going."

articles.title: Prince William makes surprise appearance on Graham Norton
articles.summary: The Prince of Wales was marking his Earthshot Prize, to which all of Norton's guests were linked.
articles.body:
The Prince of Wales has made a surprise appearance on the Graham Norton Show, as part of a special edition to mark the Earthshot Prize.

During the episode, which airs on Friday, he joined Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham, who are all involved with the prize.

As Norton spoke about the initiative with the trio he surprised the audience by then inviting the prince out to join them on the sofa.

They discussed the need to pair optimism and urgency when tackling climate change. The prize was founded by William to "celebrate and scale the solutions that will repair our planet".

The guests also chatted about William's long-time support for Aston Villa, and his love of Christopher Nolan films.

William set up the Earthshot Prize in 2020, drawing inspiration from US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely.

There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate. Each winner receives £1m.

The future king has committed himself to the prize until 2030. This year's winners will be announced at a ceremony in Mumbai in November.

Last year, the ceremony for the prizes drew famous faces such as former Formula 1 driver Sebastian Vettel and then-UK prime minister Keir Starmer. Pop stars Kylie Minogue and Shawn Mendes performed at the ceremony in Rio de Janeiro.

The 2025 winners included Lagos Fashion Week, for "transforming one of the world's most wasteful industries" by requiring designers to demonstrate their commitment to sustainability.

At last year's ceremony, William said the winners were "proof that progress is possible".

The Graham Norton Show is on BBC One at 22.40 Friday.

articles.title: Magnitude 7 earthquake kills 16 people in China’s Tibet, Xinhua reports
articles.summary: The powerful earthquake has killed 16 people and wounded 32 so far, local medics reported.
articles.body:
A magnitude 7 earthquake hit China’s southwestern region of Tibet at around 10:33 p.m. (1433 GMT) on Thursday, killing 16 people and injuring 32 others, state ‌news agency Xinhua reported, citing Nagqu City’s emergency management bureau.

11 of the injured were in serious condition while 21 sustained minor injuries, Xinhua added.

A level-II earthquake disaster emergency response was activated in the area, the news agency said.

The US Geological Survey said that the earthquake’s epicentre was in a mountainous area about 190 kilometres east-northeast of Nagqu, and 390 kilometres northeast of the regional capital Lhasa.

Local authorities have found at least two people injured in a village near the epicentre, with some houses in villages closest to the epicentre showing cracks, according to Xinhua.

Videos released by local official media showed people leaving their ⁠homes and seeking shelter outside or in ⁠their cars parked on the street.

The earthquake is ‌the strongest to hit China since January 2024.

articles.summary: Western Railway’s Ratlam Division earns ₹26.96 crore by auctioning 5,000 MT scrap under Zero Scrap Campaign, clearing condemned assets and freeing yard space.

articles.title: Iran says 7 oil tankers attacked in the Strait of Hormuz as fears grow of a return to war
articles.summary: TEL AVIV, Israel — Seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz overnight after being hit by Iran or striking naval mines, Tehran said Thursday, a markedly high number as tensions rise over concerns about a return to all-out war.
articles.body: TEL AVIV, Israel — Seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz overnight after being hit by Iran or striking naval mines, Tehran said Thursday, a markedly high number as tensions rise over concerns about a return to all-out war. With days before a close election in Israel in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could lose power, and before next month’s U.S. midterm election in which war-linked high prices have sparked voter anger, there are concerns that U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran could resume. “Netanyahu wants to attack Iran, that’s not even a question,” Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies and a former Iran specialist in Israel’s military and intelligence services, told The Associated Press. He accused Israel of rushing into another round with Iran without revamping its strategy. A clear Netanyahu victory in the Oct. 27 election means an attack is almost guaranteed, he said. Main opposition candidates are likely to focus on domestic issues first, but Citrinowicz said he believed the region is on the way toward “another kinetic escalation.” Iran repeats threat to attack U.S. bases in the region Iranian state television reported the claims about the latest attacks on ships, which the AP couldn’t independently confirm. The report cited the Revolutionary Guard Corps navy, which again threatened to strike U.S. military bases in the region if the U.S. keeps helping to guide commercial ships through the strait. The report didn’t mention casualties. Iran still asserts control over the waterway, a central point of leverage in any talks with the U.S. over the war. October has had the most reported attacks on commercial shipping since March in the war’s opening weeks, according to a British military monitor, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations. UKMTO didn’t report the latest attacks, but it has noted new reluctance by some shippers to report incidents. Oil producers have found ways to keep crude flowing, experts say, but at a mounting cost. Tankers continue moving through Strait of Hormuz despite attacks Oil tankers are still moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection despite the recent upsurge in attacks, according to shipping data and analysis company Lloyd’s List Intelligence. Tanker operators willing to risk the voyage have been shuttling oil from Gulf producers through the strait at night with their location systems and mobile phones turned off using a U.S.-protected lane near the coast of Oman. Those tankers transfer oil to other tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman for shipment to customers in Asia. Those “active Gulf operators show little sign of retreating” despite 28 attacks on ships in October, the highest since the start of the war, Lloyd’s said in an online webinar Thursday. The so-called “dark shuttle” overseen by U.S. Central Command has helped return oil shipments from the Gulf at roughly prewar levels, but at high costs in time, money and sailors’ lives. Spot charter rates for tankers have soared into the hundreds of thousands of dollars a day, while the ship-to-ship transfers can take several days. U.N. urges U.S. and Iran to return to diplomacy to end conflict, reopen strait U.N. spokesman Stephane Dujarric said no commercial ships should be attacked and called for diplomacy between the U.S. and Iran to reopen the strait. “For the sake of the people of the region and for the broader world, we need to see that waterway reopen, and we need to see tensions go down,” he told reporters Thursday. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Wednesday said Tehran remains open to diplomacy, but is ready to defend itself. Iran has warned that it learned important military lessons from the war that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Feb. 28, indicating in recent days that it could expand targets to include infrastructure such as undersea cables and data centers. The United States, for its part, is sending more military assets to the region, including a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops, to join the largest force of American warships and aircraft in the Middle East in decades. Mediators, meanwhile, have been trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to formal talks. Iran still promotes its latest proposal to end the war and fully open the strait within a week if the U.S. meets several conditions, including ending the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports. It echoes conditions in the deal that fell apart within days of both sides signing it in June. U.S. President Donald Trump rejected the latest proposal last month, but both sides acknowledged that indirect discussions have continued. The stakes are even higher if all-out war resumes A return to full fighting would again endanger civilians throughout the region and complicate global deliveries of oil, natural gas and related products like fertilizer from the region and likely bring another spike in prices. The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, this week acknowledged that the Islamic Republic will suffer under a prolonged U.S. blockade. But economic pain and strategic collapse are not the same thing, he added, according to Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency. Now the conflict has widened with the recent surge in fighting between Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia. The Saudi kingdom backs a coalition of forces with Yemen’s internationally recognized government that is fighting the rebels. The Houthis’ repeated deadly attacks on airports and other facilities inside Saudi Arabia have pressured the close U.S. ally, which has sought military aid. The escalation also has threatened a crucial shipping corridor, the Bab el-Mandeb at the southern end of the Red Sea. Meanwhile, the president of Saudi oil company Aramco, whose sites have been targeted by the Houthis, said the amount of oil moving through a pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz has increased threefold in light of the global energy crisis. The East-West pipeline’s capacity has surged from two million to seven million barrels each day, Amin Nasser said in an interview with Saudi-owned television Al Arabiya Business. He said the company has been using drones to assess any damage to the pipeline and help with firefighting.
